dialogue.english: Good morning, how has your day been?
Good morning, I have spent the day well if you have spent yours well too.
I have spent the day very well.
Are you happy / well today?
Yes, I am very well.

grammar_notes.title: Subject Concords (Zvivakashure zveChiito)
grammar_notes.content: In Zezuru Shona, the 1st person singular prefix is 'ndi-' ('ndaswera' = I spent the day; 'ndinofara' = I am pleased). The polite 2nd person plural prefix is 'mu-' or 'ma-' in past tense ('maswera' = you [honorific] spent the day). Always address elders and acquaintances with the plural honorific 'mu-/ma-'.
grammar_notes.rule: Subject prefix (mu-/ndi-) + Tense sign (-a-/-no-) + Verb root (-swera/-fara)

grammar_notes.title: Tonal Patterns: Maswéra séi
grammar_notes.content: Greetings in Central Shona follow a distinct High-Low-High tone contour: 'maswéra' (L-H-L) and 'séi' (H-L). The interrogative marker 'here' carries Low tones and turns any declarative sentence into a polite question.

cultural_notes.title: Kukwazisana Setsika (Cultural Greeting Etiquette)
cultural_notes.content: In Shona tradition, one does not merely say 'Hello'. The greeting is reciprocal and inquires into well-being. Clapping hands gently (kuwombera) with cupped palms accompanied by a slight knee bend signifies deep respect (tsika nechiremerera).

active_exercises.prompt: Translate into Shona: 'Good morning, how are you (polite)?'
Ndaswera kana ________ (if you have also spent the day).

dialogue.english: What is your (polite) name?
My name is Tendai.
Where do you come from?
I come from Harare.
I am learning Shona.

grammar_notes.title: Mupanda 5 (Class 5): Zita / Mazita
grammar_notes.content: 'Zita' (name) belongs to Class 5 (Ri- / Ø- class). The possessive concord for Class 5 is 'ra-'. Thus: 'zita r-angu' (my name), 'zita r-enyu' (your [polite] name). Note that the plural is Class 6: 'mazita' with possessive concord 'a-' ('mazita edu' = our names).

grammar_notes.title: Locative Class 17: Ku-
grammar_notes.content: The prefix 'ku-' marks general or distant location or motion towards/from ('kubva kuHarare' = coming from Harare; 'kuenda kumusha' = going home).

cultural_notes.title: Kukosha kweZita (The Significance of Names)
cultural_notes.content: Shona names are meaningful sentences or invocations: 'Tendai' (Give thanks), 'Tatenda' (We are thankful), 'Rudo' (Love), 'Farai' (Rejoice). Asking someone's totem (mutupo) often follows the introduction.

active_exercises.prompt: Zita ________ ndiFarai. (My name is Farai)
active_exercises.explanation: Zita is Class 5, so it takes 'rangu'.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you ask 'Where do you come from?' politely?

dialogue.english: This is my father.
That over there is my mother.
How many younger siblings do you have?

dialogue.shona: Ndine vanun'una vaviri nemukoma mumwe chete.
dialogue.english: I have two younger siblings and only one older brother.
dialogue.literal_gloss: I-have younger-siblings two and-elder-brother one only.

grammar_notes.title: Mupanda 1 & 2: Munhu / Vanhu (People & Kinship)
grammar_notes.content: Class 1 prefix is 'mu-' (singular), Class 2 is 'va-' (plural). In respectful speech, parents are treated with Class 2 concords even in singular: 'Baba vangu' (my father), 'Amai vangu' (my mother), 'Vanhu vaviri' (two people).
grammar_notes.rule: Honorific Class 2 plural concord 'va-' applied to parents

cultural_notes.title: Ukama (Kinship Terminology)
cultural_notes.content: In Shona, kinship does not have a single generic 'brother'. 'Mukoma' is an older sibling of the same sex; 'munun'una' is a younger sibling of the same sex; 'hanzvadzi' is a sibling of the opposite sex.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate: 'This is my mother.'

dialogue.english: What are you selling today?
We have fresh sweet corn and leafy greens.
How much is one cob of corn?
It is one dollar for three thick cobs.

grammar_notes.title: Mupanda 7 & 8: Chi- / Zvi- (Artifacts & Produce)
grammar_notes.content: 'Chiguri' (maize cob, Class 7) plurals to 'zviguri' (Class 8). The numeral concord must match: 'chiguri chi-mwe' (one cob) vs 'zviguri zvi-viri' (two cobs).
grammar_notes.rule: Class 7 concord: chi- / Class 8 concord: zvi-

cultural_notes.title: Muriwo netsika dzechikafu (Greens & Relish)
cultural_notes.content: A quintessential Shona meal consists of 'Sadza' eaten with 'muriwo' (covo, rape, or pumpkin leaves cooked with peanut butter - dovi) or meat.

active_exercises.prompt: Chiguri ________ chete imarii? (one cob only)

dialogue.english: What time is it now?
It is twelve o'clock noon.
When will we see each other again?
We will see each other on Monday morning.

grammar_notes.title: Future Tense Prefix: -cha-
grammar_notes.content: The simple future tense in Zezuru Shona is formed with the infix '-cha-': 'ti-cha-onana' (we will see each other). Reciprocal verbs end in '-ana' (onana = see each other).

cultural_notes.title: Mazuva eVhiki (Days of the Week)
cultural_notes.content: Monday is 'Muvhuro' (the opening day from kuvhura = to open); Friday is 'Chishanu' (the fifth day); Sunday is 'Svondo' (from Afrikaans Sondag or Sunday church).

active_exercises.prompt: Translate: 'We will see each other on Monday.'

dialogue.english: Does this car / kombi go to the city centre?
Yes, it goes right to the middle of the city.
Get inside, the bus will leave shortly.
I request to alight at the next stop.

grammar_notes.title: Mupanda 9 & 10 (N- / Dzin- Class)
grammar_notes.content: 'Mota' (car), 'nzira' (path), 'imba' (house) belong to Class 9. The subject concord is 'i-' in present: 'mota i-no-enda' (the car goes). Demonstrative is 'iyi' (this) and 'idzo' (those, Class 10).
grammar_notes.rule: Class 9 subject concord: i- / Demonstrative: iyi

cultural_notes.title: Kombi neMabhazi (Public Transit Culture)
cultural_notes.content: Kombis (minibus taxis) and conductors (hwindi) are a hallmark of urban Zimbabwean life. Courteously asking the conductor 'Pachiteshi chiri mberi ndapota' ensures a smooth drop-off.

active_exercises.prompt: Mota ________ inoenda kuguta. (This car)

review_summary.title: Synthesis of Grammatical Classes & Conversational Zezuru

sections.heading: 1. Subject Concords & Politeness Hierarchy
points: Singular 1st person prefix is 'ndi-' ('ndaswera', 'ndinofara').
Polite 2nd person prefix is 'mu-' / 'ma-' ('maswera sei', 'munobva kupi'). Always use this with elders and new acquaintances.
Honorific plural applied to parents: 'Baba vangu', 'Amai vangu' taking Class 2 concord 'va-'.

sections.heading: 2. Noun Classes 1 through 10 Overview
points: Class 1/2: mu- / va- (munhu / vanhu) - personal nouns.
Class 5/6: ri- / ma- (zita / mazita) - possessive takes 'rangu' in cl 5.
Class 7/8: chi- / zvi- (chiguri / zviguri) - artifacts, instruments, food portions.
Class 9/10: n- / dzin- (mota / mota, imba / dzimba) - concord 'i-' / 'dzi-'.

sections.heading: 3. Tense Markers & Particles
points: Present Habitual: '-no-' ('ndinobva', 'munotengesei').
Past Stative: '-a-' ('ndaswera', 'ndatenda').
Future: '-cha-' ('tichaonana').
Enclitic '-wo' for 'also/too' ('maswerawo').
